Launch and availability

kandidaty.zagolovok: PostgreSQL 19 Released
kandidaty.tekst:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

Tags: mysql, postgresql, replication, scaling, wikipedia, ai-security-research

kandidaty.zagolovok: My wife thinks AI is a person
kandidaty.tekst:
The other day my wife was chatting with AI.

P.s. The full interactive version of this post is here.

So let’s overlook the actual impossibilities and find out.

Before we do the maths, people have been trying versions of this for 256 years.

Nearly all of them shut down or got caught. None of them came close to today’s scale.

So what would it actually take?

Let’s be generous. Assume everyone types at world-record speed, 200 words a minute, non-stop. Everyone is happy to wait 10 minutes for a reply. And it’s a remote company spread across every time zone, so someone is always awake.

The average ChatGPT user sends about 4 messages a day, and a reply is roughly 500 words now. With over a billion people using the big AI chatbots, that’s about 6 billion messages every day.

10.4 million people typing at world-record speed, round the clock, with no sleep, no lunch, and no days off.

Okay, let’s run it like a real company instead. Which means it needs a CEO. Me.

11.8 billion internal messages a day, just to keep the place running. Oh, and we still have to answer the 6 billion messages people actually sent us.

All in, you’d need 77.4 million staff just to keep 10.4 million people typing at any given moment.

If you want to check my maths: a 40-hour week, time off from a 2025 survey of UK call centres, 12.1 people per manager (the US average), and 2 HR people per 100 staff (SHRM). People quit at the US rate, earn the US median for customer service, and get 153 chat messages a day, like the average Microsoft Teams user. The biggest Zoom call holds 1 million.

More people won’t work. But what about a guessing game from 1950, played by a mathematician called Claude Shannon? Yes, Claude.

He picked a line from a book, hid it from his wife Betty, and got her to guess it one letter at a time.

Betty didn’t know the sentence, she just knew the patterns of English.

My wife does this to me every day. She’s had years of practice.

So what if we replaced Betty with a computer?

For more than 60 years, the answer was no. Giving machines more to read barely helped, because they could only see the last couple of words. Try guessing what comes after “speak fluent…” with no other clues.

In 2017, eight people at Google let it see every word at once and weigh the ones that matter, like France. They called that attention, and the machine a transformer. It’s the T in ChatGPT.

Suddenly, giving it more to read actually worked. More text, bigger brain, better guesses.

Writing a reply is the same thing. It reads what you said and guesses the next word, or piece of a word (called a token), sticks it on the end, looks back at everything again, and guesses the next one.

It’s read websites, books, forums, fan wikis, and code. A top model trains on more than 32 trillion tokens. Reading that non-stop would take you about 190,000 years.

It doesn’t store those pages to look up later like a search engine. It just keeps the patterns.

So I explained all of that to my wife.

No

kandidaty.tekst:
@AnthropicAI: Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Hermes Enterprise now works inside Microsoft Teams, the Microsoft Store and Azure. In Teams, employees hand Hermes work like financial analysis, document drafts or inbox triage, and review the result in the same chat. Agent workloads run in isolated Azure Container Apps sandboxes.
